stem.en: The SENSEX line for 1998-2026 ends many times higher than it began. Yet a saver who bought shares in 2007 and sold them a year later, in 2008 got back less money than he put in. What does this show about shares?

text.en: The index follows only thirty large companies, so money in smaller companies would not have fallen in that year.
The saver chose badly, because any other company would certainly have risen over that single year.
Shares are a poor home for money over twenty years too, because one bad year erases the whole rise.
A rise over the long run does not protect money that has to be taken out on a particular date.

explanation.en: The long-run rise describes what happened to someone who could wait out the dips. A saver who sells inside a dip gets the price of that day, so a rise over twenty-eight years says nothing about the price next year. The thirty-company point is also wrong: when the market falls, shares across the market usually fall together.

hints.en: Separate the two claims: what the line does over twenty-eight years, and what it does in the particular year the money is needed.
The saver did not sell at a good time. Does the chart promise any date on which a sale will be profitable?
